claims.text: Multilayer HEA coatings resist time-dependent plastic deformation more effectively than homogeneous HEA films of equivalent overall composition.
Chemically sharp interfaces act as barriers to dislocation motion.
Chemically sharp interfaces impede diffusion-driven processes such as dislocation climb.
Interfacial inhibition of dislocation motion and diffusion-driven processes lowers the creep strain rate.
Deposition parameters can be used to control multilayer interface chemistry and sharpness.
Creep behavior and atomic rearrangement rates are strongly governed by applied stress and temperature.
Temperatures around 500–600 °C under moderate-to-high stresses activate diffusion and dislocation climb in the proposed coatings.
Chemically sharp interfaces create robust dislocation pile-ups.
The multilayer architecture creates internal stress fields.
Interfacial barriers hinder both dislocation nucleation and dislocation motion.
The multilayer architecture reduces the rate of diffusion-mediated creep.
The interfaces increase the effective threshold stress for creep by pinning dislocations or forcing them to change paths.
Under identical temperature and stress, multilayer coatings will exhibit less creep strain or displacement than homogeneous HEA coatings.
The creep-strain reduction may be on the order of tens of percent.
The hypothesis primarily applies when diffusion and dislocation climb dominate creep, including a proposed regime around 500–600 °C.
A shift to twinning-dominated deformation could place the material outside the hypothesis's applicable regime.
A shift to phase-transformation-dominated deformation could place the material outside the hypothesis's applicable regime.
Nanoindentation creep testing can characterize time-dependent deformation at small scales in HEAs.
